title: How do you migrate a live workflow from synchronous REST to Kafka without a flag-day cutover — let both models coexist, define which is authoritative at each stage, use shadow/dual processing + idempotent consumers + feature flags to validate the event path, then transfer ownership gradually without losing or duplicating business operations?
shortTitle: How do you migrate a live workflow from synchronous REST to Kafka without a flag-day cutover
topicTitle: How do you migrate a live workflow from synchronous REST to Kafka without a flag

s1_definition.profdef: You migrate incrementally by running the synchronous REST path and the new Kafka event path side by side, with the synchronous path remaining authoritative while you validate the event path in shadow mode. The event consumers are idempotent so dual processing never double-applies, feature flags control which path is authoritative per segment, and you gradually transfer ownership by comparing outputs, ramping traffic, and only then decommissioning the old path, so no business operation is ever lost or duplicated during the transition.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants to switch from processing transfers at the old manual counter to a new automated conveyor system, but cannot shut the bank for a day to swap them. So they run both at once: the old counter still officially processes every transfer, while the new conveyor quietly processes a copy and the staff compare the two results every evening. Once the conveyor matches the counter perfectly for weeks, they let it handle ten percent of real transfers, then fifty, then all, and finally retire the counter. A unique stamp on each slip ensures no transfer is ever done twice while both run.
s1_definition.oneliner: Run both paths together with the old one authoritative, shadow-validate the Kafka path with idempotent consumers and feature flags, then ramp ownership gradually and decommission only after the event path proves equivalent.

sections.s2_technical:
The guiding principle is that a flag-day cutover, where you switch everything at once at midnight, is unacceptable for a live financial workflow because any bug means lost or duplicated money and there is no safe rollback. So the migration is a sequence of reversible stages where both models coexist and you always know which one is authoritative.

The first stage is coexistence with the synchronous path authoritative. The REST endpoint keeps doing exactly what it did and remains the source of truth for the business outcome. Alongside it, you start publishing a Kafka event describing the same operation, ideally via a transactional outbox so the event is written atomically with the business change and can never be lost. At this point the event path has no business authority; it exists only to carry the same information.

The second stage is shadow or dual processing. A new Kafka consumer processes those events into a parallel copy of the state, for example a shadow ledger table, without affecting real customers. You then run a reconciliation job that compares the shadow outcome with the authoritative outcome for every operation and reports any divergence. This is how you validate the event path against reality under full production load without risk, because the shadow result is never shown to anyone. Idempotency is non-negotiable here: the consumer must dedupe by a business key or message id so that redelivery or dual publication never double-applies, otherwise your shadow diverges for the wrong reason.

The third stage is defining authority per stage and controlling it with feature flags. You decide explicitly, for each step of the workflow, which path is authoritative, and you expose a feature flag that can flip authority for a narrow segment, such as internal test accounts first, then one percent of real customers. The flag lets you move authority from the REST path to the Kafka path gradually and, critically, flip it back instantly if reconciliation shows a problem. During this ramp you must prevent double execution: when authority moves to the event path for a request, the REST path must stop performing the business action for that request, which the feature flag coordinates.

The fourth stage is gradual ownership transfer and decommission. You ramp the flag from one percent to ten to fifty to a hundred, watching reconciliation stay clean and monitoring consumer lag, error rates, and dead-letter volume at each step. Only once the event path has been fully authoritative and proven equivalent for a sustained period do you remove the old synchronous business logic and the shadow comparison. A senior nuance is that throughout, idempotency plus a durable processed-key store is what guarantees no duplication, the outbox is what guarantees no loss, and reconciliation is what gives you the confidence to advance; the feature flag is the control surface, not the safety mechanism itself. You also keep the ability to roll back at every stage, which is the whole point of avoiding a flag day.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India processes transfers through a synchronous REST endpoint and wants to move to a Kafka-driven flow, but cannot risk losing or duplicating a single transfer during the switch. This is exactly why we run both paths with REST authoritative and Kafka in shadow first.

Problem 2 — The team needs proof the event path produces identical results before trusting it. This is exactly what shadow processing plus a reconciliation comparison provides, by running the event path into a shadow ledger and comparing every outcome.

Problem 3 — When they start trusting the event path, they must avoid processing the same transfer on both paths. This is exactly what idempotent consumers plus a feature flag deciding authority per request achieve.

Our mini-project simulates the migration. The code defines a `TransferEvent`, an authoritative `RestTransferProcessor` that updates the real ledger and publishes an event, a `ShadowConsumer` that idempotently applies events to a shadow ledger, a `Reconciler` that compares real and shadow balances, a `FeatureFlag` controlling authority and ramp percentage, and a demo that processes several transfers in shadow mode, reconciles them to prove equivalence, then flips authority to the event path for a ramped percentage.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two transfers TXF-1 and TXF-2 between SAV2001 and CUR3001, each account starting at 500000; TXF-1's event delivered twice.

Step 1: The REST processor, which is authoritative, applies TXF-1 to the real ledger, debiting SAV2001 and crediting CUR3001. It then publishes a `TransferEvent` describing the same operation for the shadow path.

Step 2: The shadow consumer receives TXF-1, claims the id for idempotency, and applies the same change to the shadow ledger. Real and shadow now match.

Step 3: TXF-2 follows the same pattern, applied authoritatively to the real ledger and mirrored to the shadow ledger.

Step 4: A duplicate TXF-1 event is published to simulate at-least-once delivery. The shadow consumer sees the id is already processed and skips it, so the shadow ledger does not double-apply and stays equivalent to the real ledger.

Step 5: The reconciler compares every account's real and shadow balance and finds them identical, so it reports equivalence, which is the signal that the event path can be trusted.

Step 6: Because reconciliation passed, the feature flag is flipped so the event path becomes authoritative and the ramp is set to ten percent. From now on a deterministic ten percent of transfers route authority to the event path, while the REST path stops performing the business action for those requests to avoid double execution.

```
2026-10-24 14:13:40 INFO    REST (authoritative) applied TXF-1 Rs.50000
2026-10-24 14:13:40 INFO    SHADOW applied TXF-1 Rs.50000
2026-10-24 14:13:40 INFO    REST (authoritative) applied TXF-2 Rs.20000
2026-10-24 14:13:40 INFO    SHADOW applied TXF-2 Rs.20000
2026-10-24 14:13:40 INFO    SHADOW duplicate TXF-1 skipped
2026-10-24 14:13:40 INFO    Reconciliation equivalent = true
2026-10-24 14:13:40 INFO    Authority ramped: event path now authoritative for 10% of traffic
```

```
  Transfer TXF-1
    │

    │ bus.publish(TransferEvent TXF-1) ─────────┐

  real ledger (source of truth)       ShadowConsumer (idempotent)
                                        │ claim TXF-1 (first) → apply

  ── Stage 3: reconcile ──
  Reconciler.compare(real, shadow) → equivalent? ──yes──┐

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The core principle I lead with is that a flag-day cutover is unacceptable for a live financial workflow, because if anything is wrong you have already lost or duplicated money and there is no safe rollback. So I migrate as a sequence of reversible stages where the synchronous REST path and the new Kafka event path coexist and I always know exactly which one is authoritative.

The first stage is coexistence with REST authoritative. The REST endpoint keeps doing its job and remains the source of truth, and alongside it I start publishing a Kafka event describing the same operation, ideally through a transactional outbox so the event is written atomically with the business change and can never be lost. At this point the event path carries information but has no business authority. The second stage is shadow or dual processing: a new idempotent consumer applies those events into a parallel shadow copy of the state, and a reconciliation job compares the shadow outcome with the authoritative outcome for every operation. That is how I validate the event path against full production reality without any customer risk, and idempotency is non-negotiable so that redelivery or dual publication never double-applies and never causes a false divergence.

The third stage defines authority per stage and controls it with feature flags. I decide explicitly which path is authoritative for each step, and a feature flag lets me move authority from REST to Kafka for a narrow, deterministic segment, starting with internal accounts then one percent of real customers. The flag coordinates the hand-off so that when authority moves to the event path for a request, the REST path stops performing the business action for that request, which is what prevents double execution. Crucially, the flag can flip authority back instantly if reconciliation ever diverges. The fourth stage is the gradual ramp from one to ten to fifty to a hundred percent, watching reconciliation stay clean and monitoring lag, error rate, and dead-letter volume, and only after the event path has been fully authoritative and equivalent for a sustained period do I remove the old synchronous logic and the shadow comparison.

On my project at National Bank of India we moved the transfer workflow exactly this way. REST stayed authoritative while we published transfer events via an outbox, an idempotent shadow consumer built a shadow ledger keyed by transfer id, and a nightly reconciler compared real and shadow balances. We proved equivalence under full load for weeks, including absorbing duplicate deliveries without divergence, then used a feature flag to ramp authority from one percent upward, with the ability to roll back instantly, and only decommissioned the old path once the event path had owned a hundred percent cleanly. The point I stress is that idempotency guarantees no duplication, the outbox guarantees no loss, reconciliation gives the confidence to advance, and the feature flag is the control surface rather than the safety mechanism itself.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I avoid a flag day by running both paths together with the old one authoritative, shadow-validating the Kafka path with idempotent consumers and a reconciler, then using feature flags to ramp authority gradually with instant rollback, so ownership transfers without ever losing or duplicating a business operation.
